text: Newcastle disease (ND) is caused by a virus, with disease severity varying by strain. In Cambodia, acute ND circulates with symptoms ranging from very high mortality to more moderate illness (death typically 1–3 days after onset); highly virulent strains cause sudden, fast-spreading mortality, sometimes with ruffled feathers, birds not eating or moving, and greenish-dark watery diarrhea; less virulent strains cause milder respiratory signs (gasping, coughing, sneezing), often followed by nervous signs like tremor and twisted neck. A sudden drop in egg production is also a warning sign. Transmission: the virus survives in the environment, especially in droppings; direct spread happens bird-to-bird via feces and respiratory discharge (buying new birds at a wet market is high-risk, since a healthy-looking bird can be incubating ND — average incubation is 5–6 days); indirect spread happens via people carrying the virus home on shoes/clothes from a market or infected farm. Necropsy findings can look like HPAI; birds infected with highly virulent strains show hemorrhagic lesions in the proventriculus, intestine, trachea, and swelling of the head/neck. Treatment: none, since it's viral; when a low-virulence strain is involved, severe illness is often really due to a concurrent bacterial infection (Mycoplasma, E. coli), and antibiotics (e.g. Doxycycline) can prevent high mortality in that case — often the underlying mild ND goes undiagnosed and only the secondary bacterial infection is identified. Prevention: for small flocks, the I2 vaccine (Navetco) is well suited since it doesn't need strict cold-chain handling and can be stored/transported at room temperature; vaccination reduces clinical signs and mortality but does not stop virus replication/shedding, so vaccinated flocks can still have milder outbreaks (flock mortality of 30–60% has been seen even in a mainly-vaccinated outbreak) — vaccinating chicks at 7 and 28 days protects them to market weight, and the I2 vaccine also spreads naturally to protect unvaccinated in-contact birds.
